newsitem.title: USA: US NAPM index may be near top of Fed comfort range.
newsitem.headline: US NAPM index may be near top of Fed comfort range.

text.p: A key U.S. manufacturing index neared a closely watched milestone on Thursday and as usual, the financial markets began worrying about whether it would prompt the Federal Reserve to raise official interest rates.
The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index of manufacturing activity came in at 54.0, nearing levels that historically have presaged credit tightenings by the Fed.
The Fed kicked off its last tightening cycle, in early 1994, when the NAPM index hit 55.3.
Four more times in 1994, and once in early 1995, the central bank hiked rates at policy meetings that followed NAPM reports ranging from 55.8 to 59.5.

Many analysts "talk about the Fed not tightening when the index is below 54.7" but raising rates when it moves higher, said Michelle Colley Laughlin, chief Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc.
A NAPM headline number of 54.0 is consistent with overall economic growth of about 3.5 percent, according to Norbert Ore, the new chairman of the NAPM's Business Survey Committee.
Such an expansion rate would overshoot the Fed's perception of the long-term sustainable, non-inflationary growth rate of about 2.0 to 2.5 percent.
The NAPM headline number, however, tells only half the story.

Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc, said Fed policymakers would ask two questions if the NAPM index were to maintain its current strength: (1) Will the growth be sustained? (2) is it inflationary?
With market interest rates shooting up quickly at the first signs of an economic growth spurt, speedy expansion would most likely be derailed, Kretzmer said.

Clues to the second question's answer can be found in the NAPM price index, which rose to 51.5 in December from 45.9 the month before. Despite the increase, the price index is nowhere near its levels during the last tightening cycle.
As the Fed raised rates between February 1994 and February 1995, the NAPM price index rose as high as 85.3 from a starting point of 58.6.
